blocks.text: In verse 17, The seeds have rotted under their clods, the storehouses are desolate, the granaries are destroyed, because the grain has withered.] In the first clause of this verse, עבשו פרדות תחת מגרפותיהם, three of the four words are found nowhere else. Hence the interpreters are at a loss here, and nowhere is there greater disagreement. For the Greeks render it Ἐσκίρτησαν δαμάλεις ἐπὶ ταῖς φάτναις [Eskirtēsan damaleis epi tais phatnais], The heifers have leapt at their mangers ^{(4)}. And Jerome: The beasts have rotted [III, 300] in their dung. And the Chaldee: אתמסיו גרבי חמר תחות מגופתהון, The jars of wine have run out under their lids ^{(5)}. And the Syriac again differently ^{(6)}. We, with the Hebrews: The seeds have rotted under their clods. That is, עבשׁו is the same as עפשׁו, with Beth and Pe interchanged, letters which are homogeneous and easily interchangeable. Further, in the Talmudists עפשׁ means to rot. So Jerome rightly has computruerunt [have rotted]. And that פרדות is truly to be explained as seeds is suggested by the fact that in Syriac ܦܪܕܬܐ is a seed. Hence in the Syriac version, Matth. XIII, 31, ܦܪܕܬܐ ܕܚܪܕܠܐ is a grain of mustard seed; Ioh. XII, 24, ܦܪܕܬܐ ܕܚܛܬܐ, a grain of wheat; 1 Corinth. XV, 37, ܦܪܕܬܐ ܕܚܛܬܐ ܘܕܣܥܪܐ, grains of wheat and of barley ^{(7)}. Finally, that מגרפות are clods [III, 301] is suggested by the similarity of the words גרף (whence מגרפות) and רגב, the latter of which occurs twice in Job for clod. And indeed clods seem to be called מגרפות from the verb גרף, which, used of a torrent, means to carry away. Thus Iud. V, 21: the torrent Kishon גרפם, swept them away. And in Arabic, in Alcamus: جرفته السيل [jarafathu al-sayl], the torrent swept him away; سيل جراف [sayl jurāf], a torrent sweeping everything away; جرف [jurf], a clod of earth which a torrent carries away. Thus מגרפות are properly רגבי נחל, clods of the torrent, as they are called in Iob. XXI, 33, and then also clods of any kind ^{(8)}. Further, grains (or seeds) [III, 302] usually rot under their clods (that is, when cast into the ground) when the [col. 472] rains are excessive. Hence Pliny, book 10, chapter 24, wants sowing in humid places [III, 303] to be done earlier, lest the seed rot from the rain. And Kimchi on this passage of Joel: יתעפשו גרגרי הזרע מפני הגשמים, The grains of seed rot because of the rains ^{(9)}. And Junius: The sown crops have become mouldy from excessive rains, which spoil the seed. In the same sense the distinguished Diodati: Accenni che le semente sarebbero guaste da soverchie piogge ^{(10)}. But this does not agree with what follows, where extreme drought is described. For this is what verse 19 refers to: Fire has consumed the pastures of the wilderness, and flame has scorched all the trees of the field. And verse 20: Even the beasts of the field cry to you, because the channels of water have dried up and fire has consumed the pastures of the wilderness. Fire and flame, that is, excessive heat. As in Psal. LXXXII, 13. (var. LXXXIII, 15.): As fire burns the forest, and flame sets the mountains ablaze. Hence places parched by the heat of the sun are called חררים in Ierem. XVII, 6., that is, burning or scorched. So the rotting of the sown crops of which Joel speaks comes not from rains but from extreme drought. By this, if we wish to speak properly, seeds are said not so much to rot as to come to nothing. Pliny, in the place cited above: The reason for sowing earlier in humid places is lest the seed rot from the rain; in dry places later, so that rains may follow, lest, lying long and not germinating, it come to nothing. Such is what he said in the preceding chapter, that harmful winds empty the grains. But whether the grains rot from rain or come to nothing from drought, the Hebrew עבש, or עבש, could cover both ^{(11)}.
